children: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may announce measures to manage surplus liquidity alongside a likely rate hike at the October 7 policy outcome, with market participants divided over whether the central bank should opt for temporary tools or a more durable measure such as a cash reserve ratio (CRR) increase. According to the RBI’s latest data, the liquidity surplus in the banking system stood at Rs 5.03 lakh crore on Tuesday.

Variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) operations and sell-buy foreign exchange swaps are among the temporary options being discussed, while some market participants see a case for an incremental CRR (ICRR) or a 50-basis-point increase in CRR.
Gaura Sengupta, Chief Economist at IDFC First Bank, favours temporary measures, arguing that much of the current surplus is likely to drain naturally in the coming months.

“There is around Rs 5-6 lakh crore of surplus liquidity currently, but a large part of this is transient. By March, around Rs 4 lakh crore can be taken out through currency leakage. The RBI should therefore use temporary tools such as sell-buy swaps with maturities within FY27 or instruments with a sunset clause.”
A treasury head at a private bank also expects limited action, saying the RBI may not need to announce a permanent liquidity measure when the surplus is expected to decline further.
“I am not expecting any major announcement on liquidity. We are almost Rs 5 lakh crore in excess liquidity right now, which will probably get consumed by December, around the next policy.”
The treasury head said the RBI could consider an incremental CRR on new deposits, but only if it comes with a defined reversal window.
“An incremental CRR on the deposits that have come in could be considered for the time being, but only with a reversal window. That would make it a temporary measure.”
CRR option remains on table
A more aggressive option could be a 50-basis-point increase in CRR, which would absorb liquidity without requiring further open market operation (OMO) sales.

Abhishek Upadhyay, Executive Vice President and Co-Head of Economics and Fixed Income Research at ICICI Securities Primary Dealership, said, “On liquidity, the current surplus of around ₹4 lakh crore is not very high, although core liquidity remains above ₹10 trillion. The RBI’s comfort threshold and its choice of tools will be important. Given the market impact of recent OMO sales and FX interventions, a 50-basis-point CRR hike could be more effective in absorbing liquidity and would reinforce the signal that inflation risks remain a concern.”

The last time the RBI had revised CRR upwards was in May 21, 2022, when it was hiked by 50 basis points from 4.00 percent to 4.50 percent to absorb excess liquidity and manage inflation. Since then, the RBI has exclusively reduced the CRR, first lowering it to 4.00 percent in late 2024, followed by a phased 100-basis-point reduction throughout late 2025 that brought it down to its current 3.00 percent level.
FCNR(B) inflows created an unusual liquidity surplus

The liquidity overhang followed the strong response to the RBI’s concessional FCNR(B) swap facility. Banks mobilised $127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits by August 31, as part of total foreign-currency inflows of $136.38 billion through the special facilities.

A key feature of the FCNR(B) mobilisation was that the deposits raised under the scheme were exempt from CRR and SLR requirements. As a result, the inflows did not create a corresponding reserve requirement for banks even as the subsequent dollar-rupee swaps released rupee liquidity into the banking system.

Surplus liquidity crossed Rs 11 lakh crore in early September, prompting the RBI to conduct VRRR auctions and announce Rs 1 lakh crore of OMO sales. System liquidity has since moderated to around Rs 5 lakh crore.
Liquidity is expected to tighten

The current surplus is also expected to reduce without a large permanent intervention because several factors will naturally drain liquidity over the next few months. Currency in circulation typically rises towards the second half of the financial year, while a negative balance of payments and capital-account flows can also withdraw liquidity from the banking system.

Sengupta estimates that currency leakage alone could absorb around Rs 4 lakh crore by March. At the same time, deposit growth has been lagging credit growth, which means banks are funding a larger share of incremental lending from existing liquidity rather than fresh deposits.
The private-bank treasury head expects this process to bring the current surplus down substantially by the next policy.

This is why market participants see a stronger case for temporary liquidity measures, if required, rather than another large and permanent absorption operation. As Sengupta put it, much of the excess liquidity already created by the FCNR(B) inflows has been taken out, while the remaining surplus is expected to be gradually absorbed through these natural drains.

title: RBI MPC: CRR, VRRR, FX swaps among liquidity measures RBI may announce
